title: Dilemma Attacks
shortDefinition: A dilemma is two or more threats where defending one line exposes another.
whyItMatters: At higher levels, opponents do not give single finishes; you need chains based on reactions.
deepExplanation: Good dilemmas start from control. In back control, defending the neck exposes arm trap; clearing hooks exposes mount. Attacking becomes designed bad choices, not luck.
beginnerView: Prepare the second attack when the first is blocked.
advancedView: Build branches where every defense keeps you in a better hierarchy.

ifThenExamples.if: If you lose Dilemma Attacks during the exchange.
ifThenExamples.then: Stop accelerating, recover the nearest body structure, then continue the technique.
ifThenExamples.why: Modern no-gi punishes forceful continuation after structure is lost.

ifThenExamples.if: If the opponent correctly answers your first line.
ifThenExamples.then: Use Dilemma Attacks to switch to a safer branch instead of forcing the same line.
ifThenExamples.why: A good concept turns the opponent’s reaction into information for the next decision.

commonMisunderstandings.misunderstanding: Dilemma Attacks is a single technical trick.
commonMisunderstandings.correction: Treat it as a decision rule that appears across many positions.

commonMisunderstandings.misunderstanding: Understanding the concept automatically makes it work live.
commonMisunderstandings.correction: The concept needs body signals, short cues, and positional rolling.

trainingCues: Name Dilemma Attacks before adding force.
Find the body signal instead of guessing generally.
If structure is lost, reset one layer first.
Drill slowly, then test with progressive resistance.
